en: A Discussion on the Mind-Dharma Transmitted Apart from the Three Vehicles, by Feishan Mozhi of Fudang. Composed by Jiezhu.
Some claim that the mind-dharma transmitted apart from the teachings of the Three Vehicles is the "Ancestral Way" (Zudao). Feishan Mozhi says: This is not so.
Furthermore, that which is expounded by the Three Vehicles is but the single mind; the Dharma of the single mind is the very foundation of the teachings.
How could there be a mind apart from the mind, and yet another mind exist? Please allow me to discuss this briefly.

When the Tathāgata had entered parinirvāṇa at the city of Kuśinagara, his five hundred disciples lost their point of reliance and likewise desired to enter nirvāṇa following him. At that time, Mahākāśyapa stepped forward...
The Way [of the Buddha] said: "Do not enter nirvana until the Dharma-treasury has been compiled. He first commanded Ānanda to compile the Tathāgata’s Sūtra-piṭaka;
Upāli and others compiled the Vinaya-piṭaka; thereafter, he himself compiled the Abhidharma-piṭaka.
Since the compilation of the Tripiṭaka began with Kāśyapa, he was designated as the First Patriarch. Kāśyapa said: "It is only now that I have begun..."
To repay the Buddha’s kindness, the five hundred disciples who participated in the compilation likewise said: "That which was compiled previously is the Dharma.
All Buddhas of the three periods who realize Bodhi do so by means of this; the bodhisattvas of the ten directions cultivate and understand it by means of this.
Only this Dharma is shared by every Buddha; we have never heard of any other separate Dharma apart from this."
Kāśyapa [received it]; Kāśyapa in turn transmitted it to Ānanda; Ānanda transmitted it to Śāṇakavāsin. Is it anything other than this?
It is what is called the Dharma of the Three Piṭakas. Those who aspire to the Buddha-way rely upon it.

Relying on it as a lamp and a scale, when there are matters of doubt, they consult it to determine their weight; when there are principles that are obscure, they approach it to illuminate and clarify them.
Taking these as one's precepts, as meditative concentration, as dhāraṇī, and as the Guhyasamāja (Miyōng), one extends them through the six perfections and expands them through the myriad practices.
One is aided by the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment—namely, the faculties, powers, and limbs of awakening—and thereby brings them forth.

Having brought them forth and attained them, there arise what are called the fruits, the realizations, the three stages of worthiness, and the ten stages of sanctity. Thus, [one attains] the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the ten...
Regarding the eight extraordinary powers of the superknowledges and the attainment of supreme perfect enlightenment, which is called "the peerless," by what means is this achieved?
It is through the Teaching. As for the Teaching, it refers to the cultivation of the Path. One who studies the Sage must not be separated from it.
They depart from the truth to become Māras, externalists, and proponents of heterodox views;
such as Pūraṇa Kāśyapa and the ninety-six kinds of dissenting sects, who are born with their arms crossed [in opposition]. The Tathāgata once said to Ānanda:

"After my parinirvāṇa, these various heterodox groups will flourish in the world, concealing their deceit while claiming to be spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra). Śāṇakavāsin was about to enter parinirvāṇa.
Nirvāṇa. Furthermore, the Fourth Patriarch Upagupta said: "The Tathāgata’s various Jātaka sūtras, as well as the Vinaya and other teachings, number one hundred and seventy thousand [verses].
You must protect them so that Māras and non-Buddhists do not cause confusion and disorder.

Ten generations later, during the time of Aśvaghoṣa, heterodox paths will gradually arise; Aśvaghoṣa shall discern and refute them, taking the Laṅkāvatāra and Vaipulya sūtras as his primary authority."
He composed various treatises. Nāgārjuna was born after Aśvaghoṣa and arose as his successor; the works he produced were twice as many [as those of his predecessor].
His primary authority was the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras. Treatises such as the *Bhaya-vyūha* (The Array of Fear) and others numbered in the millions.
From the beginning, he never uttered a single word for his own private benefit; the intent of the Vaipulya (Mahāyāna) teachings was present therein.

His tears [wiped away] defilements as he succeeded to the lineage and manifested transformation through the person of Devadatta and Rāhula. For twenty-seven generations, from first to last, the flow of his transformative influence spread ever more widely.
Regarding that teaching, he was earnestly diligent, not daring to depart from it, nor daring to use external force to constrain it, but rather encouraging others with it.
Reflect upon this. He revealed its profound essence to circulate it; even when he had finished, he felt that a single day was still insufficient. When asked the reason for this, he said:
"Even the sages of the Ten Stages do not dare to depart from the various teachings; how could I dare to depart from them and consider myself sufficient?
At the moment of transmission, he would invariably say: "These are the Dharmas of the Tripitaka, which the Tathāgata transmitted to Mahākāśyapa, and Kāśyapa entrusted them to..."
Ānanda, this lineage of cotton thread has been passed down successively until it reaches me. I now, in turn, entrust this Dharma to you;
you must protect it. What are the so-called Three Piṭakas? They are the Sūtra, the Vinaya, and the Abhidharma. Their texts are vast and extensive.
All [these teachings] were present in the land of India. Bodhidharma traveled tens of thousands of li to come to Liang, braving various hardships and perils;

yet he could not transmit everything in its entirety. He bestowed upon him (Huikong) only four fascicles of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*. Huikong said, "Rely on the teaching to awaken to the essence," and further said, "Virtuous one, rely on this for practice;
you shall naturally attain deliverance from the world. From that time on, the transmission was fulfilled. Mǎn transmitted it...

At that time, under the great propagation of the Mahāyāna teachings, there were several hundred who transmitted the Dharma-nature school (Xingzong). The flourishing of these public lectures was such that... [Note: The character "燦" is omitted and replaced by "滿" as indicated in the prompt.
...the transmission of the lineage continued from master to disciple. The prosperity of these lecture assemblies reached its peak.
Because Chan did not reach full completion, his original biography refers to him as "Man" (the full name).

Now, what is called the "School of Nature" (Xingzong) is the "School of Mind" (Xinzong)—that is to say, the essential purport of the oral transmissions and texts of the patriarchs such as Nāgārjuna and Aśvaghoṣa.

Du Yu of Jinchang, regarding the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* as his own school’s tradition, noted that although this single scripture had been translated four times, it had remained obscure in the world and its profound meaning had not yet been fully elucidated.
Only the Dharma Master Bodhidharma regarded it as the "Mirror of the Mind," causing it to circulate in succession and ensuring its preservation without interruption.
The chroniclers of that time have recorded these events in detail, appending them to the various historical records and biographies.

This is truly so that those in future generations who speak of the ancestral Way shall not deviate from the scriptures, nor stray from the sages, nor allow themselves to be led astray by those who, with clever sophistry, confuse scholars and cause their minds to be troubled in myriad ways.
For a beginner in the faith, the mind is like a wind-wheel or a hair-circle (*keśonduka*); a hair-circle is easily moved, and the wind—
The wheel turns easily; as it turns and moves, its direction has no fixed reliance. One may drift into the realm of celestial Māras, or mistakenly enter the paths of externalists (*tīrthika*).
To reject the origins of Māras and externalists, and to cultivate that which the *Luo* [Lokottaravādins? study, there is only the discernment found in the Teaching.
Therefore, the Teaching is the path entered by the thirty-third patriarch of the world, and the fifty-first stage of Bodhi...
The root of the Buddha’s attainment of enlightenment must now have a successor. To succeed the Buddha is to relinquish [all attachments]; this is what the Buddhist teaching calls "the mind.
Indeed, toward the end of the Tang dynasty, as the distance from the Buddha grew ever greater, the tenets practiced and the prevailing inclinations became increasingly divergent.

Nanquan Puyuan, seizing the moment, cultivated these differences to sweep away all fundamental [attachments]. From this, the doctrine of the "Separate Transmission" arose. Puyuan having proclaimed it—
In the past, those such as Yi Xuan and Xuanchang followed in the footsteps of Zhu Fashen; in later times, they further undermined the scriptural teachings and slandered the sages and worthies.

They claimed that the teachings were but the crude fabrications of ghosts and spirits. Unable to achieve stability, their minds ran wild and perverse, appearing to devote themselves to the doctrines of the non-Buddhist Nirgranthas (Jainas).
These are not the words of the śramaṇa sons of Śākyamuni. How could those with discernment not feel heartache at this?

If you, my fellow seekers, are sinners of the Semblance Dharma who do not delight in study and do not understand the fundamental source, you are insufficient for discourse on the Tathāgata’s teaching.
Indeed, that which the Tathāgata perceives as being induced by the inverted states of the three realms and nine stages is but the single mind.

That which is transformed by the surging and submerging of the waves of the four modes of birth and the six destinies is but the single consciousness. The transformations of consciousness and mind are without end; they are characterized by arising and ceasing.
The number of these [teachings] is inexhaustible. By means of the inexhaustible Dharma, one accords with inexhaustible capacities.

Therefore, its teachings possess both the provisional and the real, as well as the sudden and the gradual; its essential purports possess both the concealed and the revealed, and the doctrine of the secret.

That which is "mind-only" is the revealed teaching; that which is not "mind-only" is the concealed teaching. If it can be revealed to someone, it is revealed; if it cannot yet be revealed to someone, then...
It is concealed. That which is kept secret and not disclosed is the "secret. Concealment reveals the secret;
thus it is called [the teaching] according to the capacity [of the recipient]. It is that which is bestowed upon those whose vessels are ready.

The former sages [held that] from the first assembly at the site of the Tathāgata’s enlightenment until the river Ajitavatī, during the forty-nine years before he taught [the Lotus Sūtra], all that was spoken was extremely subtle. As for those whom he saved...

From the ultimate to the mundane, whether small or great, coming or going, opening or closing, provisional or real, partial or complete—when one considers even a single character as a phenomenon external to the mind, it is seen that all phenomena are merely what is manifested, and all capacities are merely what is suited;

whether among devas or humans, or within the four modes of birth and six realms of existence, among the myriad billions of species and their retributions for good and evil karma, there is not a single thing that does not arise from the mind. Therefore:

It is said: "The three realms are but the one mind; the myriad dharmas are but the one consciousness. For those who study the Buddha, they take this as their standard for the teachings of the Three Vehicles;
how could there be even a trace of error here? Who would dare to claim that there is a single dharma existing apart from the mind?

To speak of a dharma-realm outside the mind is something unheard of in the path of the Buddhas. Alas, how can those of shallow and superficial understanding fail to exhaustively investigate the profound depths?
Not reaching far, [your] thoughts are shallow. What dharma was it that the First Patriarch Kāśyapa collected?
What was it that Nāgārjuna and Aśvaghoṣa described? As for your own tonsure, whom did you follow as your teacher?

And what teaching did that teacher study? Yet you proceed to reject the worthy and revile the sages; you are狂悖 (mad and perverse), stubbornly clinging to your own ignorance and meanness, opening up your own school.

They set up windows and lattices; they employ hooks, awls, concealed points, and blunt strikes. This extends to using refined phrases, obscure language, insults, and mutual attacks, vying with one another in their efforts to seize the pivot of victory and defeat.
They employ cleverness regarding gain and loss as the mechanism for victory and defeat;
this cleverness is my own delusion. It is the principle of arising and ceasing. To take the principle of arising and ceasing as the means for transcendence—
Yet, as they approach the Buddha-way, they are almost like those who retreat while running, looking back toward where they have come from;
not only do they have no means [to reach it], but in doing so, their bodies become exhausted and their tracks fall into the pits and ditches that follow them.

This is because the Buddha-way is subtle and profound, and only through wisdom can one attain harmony. Those who are alike are guided by it, and those who differ are instructed by it. Because they are instructed yet do not reflect upon it, therefore—
Deliberate upon it. To deliberate is to discern. In discerning, one must not allow private bias. This fundamental equanimity is the state of the Sage.
The Sage’s law is rooted in the Sūtras. The Sūtra says: "If sentient beings, though seeking a virtuous friend, encounter error, it is not the fault of the sentient beings.
It further says: "If practitioners are unable to achieve Unsurpassed Bodhi, even to the point of attaining only the [lesser] Śrāvaka [vehicle], [it is not their fault]."
I have heard that the Pratyekabuddhas, as well as the non-Buddhist practitioners, the various devas, the Māras, and their retinues, all fail because they do not recognize the two fundamental roots.

Their confused cultivation is like boiling sand in hopes of producing a fine meal; even if it were to pass through kalpas as numerous as dust motes, they would ultimately never succeed. Alas! How tragic this is!

The refutation and clarification are meritorious. The text states: "How great is the disparity between the Chan of antiquity and the Chan of today! Their names and realities are as far apart as the poles.
What was called 'Chan' in antiquity refers to those who rely upon the teachings to practice Chan. What is called 'Chan' today refers to those who abandon the teachings to discourse on Chan.
Those who discourse on Chan cling to the name while neglecting the reality; those who practice Chan follow the explanations [of the teachings]..."
He grasped its essential meaning and sought to remedy the contemporary malady of hypocrisy while restoring the refined and pure Way of the ancient sages;

in this regard, Master Zhugu’s critical analysis reached its ultimate perfection. Recently, the Emperor of the Great Liao issued an edict ordering the śramaṇas specializing in doctrinal studies, Quanjiao and others, to recompile the catalog of scriptures.
Consequently, works such as the so-called *Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch* and the *Baolin Zhuan* were all consigned to the flames.
To eliminate such falsehoods and delusions, the regulations have been revised and recorded in detail within the three volumes of the *Revised Zhenyuan Continuation Record*.
This clearly reveals the Buddha’s heart of entrustment and the emperors’ will to propagate and protect the Dharma.
Yet, as for the Chan school texts currently practiced in China, they frequently involve heterodox elements; this is why the masters of the Eastern Sea harbor doubts regarding the Middle Kingdom.
There was no one [to record this]. Upon seeing the lofty discourse of Feishan, I then learned that there was indeed the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla.
Yesterday, having received the King’s decree to engrave this upon a jade stele, I feared that its circulation might not be widespread; thus, I have carved it onto a wooden board. Alas!
Will those who uphold the Dharma in the final age a hundred generations hence not rely upon the power of Master Zhu? — Yi Tian, Prince of Goryeo and State Preceptor.
Text for the Memorial Sacrifice for Master Huaiyao (This text differs from the previous one, yet its purport is largely the same; therefore, it is appended here now.
In the [blank] month, Jie Zhu, a Dharma-transmitting śramaṇa serving as the abbot of Xuansha, respectfully addresses the memorial for Master Huaiyao.
The clouds of the great chiliocosm pervade the entire realm, yet only the Buddha is truly holy. Even so, he spoke of how all who have life must follow it with death. How could this be otherwise?
Now, the wise man preserves his longevity through his shared spiritual renown; his fame spreads throughout the southern regions, and his Way reaches the western frontiers.

His fragrant influence has endured for five generations, and he is indeed a worthy successor to the Dharma. Having now reached the age of eighty, his spirit remains untroubled and his faculties—sight and hearing—remain unimpaired.
In his dignified deportment and every movement, he serves as a model for his time. At the head of the era of Great Peace, he accords with the multitude; he gathers them together and leads them all.
Dong Huangbo occupied seven successive positions; his reputation and influence were widespread and pervasive. Toward the end of his life, he once again presided over the ocean of the Dharma.

He nurtured the multitude with compassion and softened the common people with forbearance. Although fierce and stubborn winds of custom had long since arisen, he always maintained that the Buddhist Way has no fixed destination other than within oneself.
What is guarded against is the passions; what is awakened to is the mind. Thus, there is the provisional and thus, there is the real. The myriad paths—
To open the oral tradition within one’s own mind is what constitutes attainment. As for those patriarchs—Aśvaghoṣa, Nāgārjuna, and Gaṇadeva—what was their method?
Some composed various treatises to explain the sūtras; others took the sūtras as their primary authority to compose treatises.

They had no private basis and were not attached to themselves; they employed skillful dialectic to mutually critique one another. Thus, even through the chaos of the Five Dynasties, [the Dharma] ultimately... (text ends).

There arose a band of deceitful followers who, seizing upon a precarious opportunity, falsely claimed that the scriptures were stolen by thieves and that the teachings of the sages and worthies were transmitted separately from the Buddhist doctrine.
They asserted that outside of Buddhism there was a distinct transmission of the mind-dharma (*cittadharma*). Now, the illumination of the Buddha’s teaching is like the sun;
the Way of the Buddha is as lofty as heaven. Heaven cannot be transgressed, and the light of the sun cannot be obscured. Only its loftiness can be matched.
One may cover [the truth], yet to accept such covering without realizing it stems from folly; one may rely on light, yet to remain unaware of it stems from blindness.

Being nothing but blind and foolish, who would investigate? Who would reflect? Having failed to cultivate the faculties and powers, and being darkened by the habitual tendencies of a lack of concentration and wisdom, you merely scold, revile, strike, and beat me.
Utterly deranged and muddled, I shall die in vain. My teacher has repeatedly instructed me with these words, and since I—
Who would dare forget what is preserved herein? It is hoped that we shall eventually behold the Buddha to evaluate the origins of this undertaking.
